match.reason: Neither bank point teaches the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, which was a separate 1918 treaty between Soviet Russia and the Central Powers, so the new point needs its own card, and the Versailles and postwar settlement points cover different treaties.

draft.title: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
card: The Bolsheviks took power in November 1917 (October in the old Russian calendar). They had promised peace, and the army was worn out and falling apart after years of heavy losses.
Talks with Germany and its allies were held at Brest-Litovsk. The Bolsheviks hoped to delay and win better terms. Trotsky led the Russian side for much of the talks.
When Germany resumed its advance in February 1918, the Bolsheviks gave in. The treaty was signed in March 1918, and Russia left the war.

Russia gave up large territories in the west, including Poland, the Baltic lands and Ukraine. These held much of its farmland, industry and population. Many Bolsheviks and their opponents saw the terms as harsh, but Lenin argued that peace was needed to keep the revolution alive.
draft.remember: Lenin accepted a harsh peace with Germany to end the war and keep Bolshevik power.

a.q: Why did Lenin accept the harsh terms of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk?
opts: He believed peace was needed to save Bolshevik rule
He thought Germany would soon lose the war anyway
He wanted Russia to keep its western farmland and industry
He had promised the Allies that Russia would stay in the war
a.why: Lenin argued that the army was broken and the revolution could not survive more fighting. Accepting the terms ended the war and protected Bolshevik power. The treaty did not keep Russia's western lands, as it gave up many of them.
a.clue: Think about the state of the army and what the Bolsheviks most needed to protect.

b.q: In 1918, Olga, a Bolshevik, says: "The treaty is a disaster, but we must sign." Which reason best fits her view?
opts: The loss of land hurts, but ending the war secures our rule
The land lost is small, so signing costs us very little
Signing will win the support of Russia's former allies
Refusing will make Germany give back our western lands
b.why: Olga sees the treaty as costly, since Russia lost large territories, yet she accepts it to end the war and secure Bolshevik rule. The claim that the losses were small is wrong, because the lost land held much of Russia's farmland, industry and population.
b.clue: Her words admit a loss but still argue for signing.

a.best: He believed peace was needed to save Bolshevik rule

b.best: The loss of land hurts, but ending the war secures our rule

problems.detail: Olga calls the treaty 'a disaster' but says 'we must sign', and the clue repeats that her words admit a loss yet argue for signing. Only one option both admits a loss and supports signing, so a student can match the quote's wording without knowing why Lenin accepted the treaty.
